span.label: what the intention-to-treat principle is, what it buys, what it costs, and where the guidelines disagree about applying it
span.quote: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) often suffer from two major complications, i.e., noncompliance and missing outcomes. One potential solution to this problem is a statistical concept called intention-to-treat (ITT) concept.

span.label: assembles the definitions of ITT, per-protocol, modified ITT and the full analysis set side by side with the regulator that issues each, and reports that the modified variant has no consistent definition at all
span.quote: It is a subset of the ITT population and allows the exclusion of some randomized subjects in a justified way (such as patients who were deemed ineligible after randomization or certain patients who never started treatment). However, the definition given to the modified ITT (mITT) in randomized controlled trial has been found to be irregular and arbitrary because there is a lack of consistent guidelines for its application. The mITT analysis allows a subjective approach in entry criteria, which may lead to confusion, inaccurate results and bias.

span.quote: Committee for Proprietary Medicinal Products (CPMP) note for guidance “Biostatistical Methodology in Clinical Trials for Marketing Authorisations for Medicinal Products” states that decisions concerning the analysis population should be guided by the principles underlying the “intention-to-treat” and the “per-protocol” strategies. When the ITT and per-protocol (PP) analyses come to essentially the same conclusions, confidence in the study results is increased.

span.label: **THE DEFINITION IS A TRIPLE REFUSAL TO CONDITION ON ANYTHING THAT HAPPENED AFTER RANDOMISATION** - `REGARDLESS OF their adherence with the entry criteria, REGARDLESS OF the treatment they actually received, and REGARDLESS OF subsequent withdrawal from treatment or deviation from the protocol`
span.quote: According to Fisher et al . (1990), the ITT analysis includes all randomized patients in the groups to which they were randomly assigned, regardless of their adherence with the entry criteria, regardless of the treatment they actually received, and regardless of subsequent withdrawal from treatment or deviation from the protocol.

span.label: and the reason is that the alternative destroys what randomisation bought: `If noncompliant subjects and dropouts are EXCLUDED from the final analysis, it might create IMPORTANT PROGNOSTIC DIFFERENCES among treatment groups` - and subjects `may be noncompliant or may drop out DUE TO THEIR RESPONSE OF TREATMENT`
span.quote: ITT analysis reflects the practical clinical scenario because it admits noncompliance and protocol deviations. ITT analysis maintains prognostic balance generated from the original random treatment allocation. It gives an unbiased estimate of treatment effect.

span.label: **THE COST IS PAID IN THE SAME COIN.** `In ITT analysis, estimate of treatment effect is generally CONSERVATIVE because of DILUTION due to noncompliance` - the property that makes it unbiased is the property that makes it small
span.quote: To begin with, if a subject who actually did not receive any treatment is included as a subject who received treatment, then it indicates very little about the efficacy of the treatment. In ITT analysis, estimate of treatment effect is generally conservative because of dilution due to noncompliance.

span.label: so the criticism is symmetrical: ITT `has been criticized for being TOO CAUTIOUS and thus being MORE SUSCEPTIBLE TO TYPE II ERROR`
span.quote: ITT analysis has been criticized for being too cautious and thus being more susceptible to type II error.

span.label: **AND THE TWO POPULATIONS FAIL IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS, WHICH IS WHY THE CHOICE IS NOT NEUTRAL.** `ITT tends to make the two treatments LOOK SIMILAR, WHEREAS the PP removes patients who do not complete treatment and is MORE ABLE TO REFLECT TREATMENT DIFFERENCES`
span.quote: ITT tends to make the two treatments look similar, whereas the PP removes patients who do not complete treatment and is more able to reflect treatment differences.

span.label: **THE MODIFIED VARIANT HAS NO STABLE DEFINITION AT ALL** - `the definition given to the modified ITT (mITT) in randomized controlled trial has been found to be IRREGULAR AND ARBITRARY because there is a LACK OF CONSISTENT GUIDELINES for its application. The mITT analysis ALLOWS A SUBJECTIVE APPROACH IN ENTRY CRITERIA`
span.quote: It is a subset of the ITT population and allows the exclusion of some randomized subjects in a justified way (such as patients who were deemed ineligible after randomization or certain patients who never started treatment). However, the definition given to the modified ITT (mITT) in randomized controlled trial has been found to be irregular and arbitrary because there is a lack of consistent guidelines for its application. The mITT analysis allows a subjective approach in entry criteria, which may lead to confusion, inaccurate results and bias.

span.label: and it is not one population but many: `multiple mITT populations CAN BE DEFINED FOR A SINGLE STUDY such as clinical mITT and microbiological mITT`
span.quote: It is mostly used in anti-infective trials where multiple mITT populations can be defined for a single study such as clinical mITT and microbiological mITT.

span.label: **THE SAME OBJECT CARRIES A THIRD NAME FROM A THIRD AUTHORITY** - ICH E9 `uses the term FULL ANALYSIS SET to describe the analysis set which is as complete as possible and AS CLOSE AS POSSIBLE TO THE ITT IDEAL`
span.quote: The International Conference on Harmonisation (ICH) E9 guideline on “Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials” uses the term “full analysis set” to describe the analysis set which is as complete as possible and as close as possible to the ITT ideal of including all randomized subjects.

span.label: **The guidelines do not agree about where the principle applies.** `Whereas the importance of the ITT population analysis in superiority designs has been well accepted, however THERE IS NO CONSENSUS ABOUT ITS ROLE IN NON-INFERIORITY TRIALS`
span.quote: CPMP guideline states that for a superiority trial, the ITT analysis should be considered primary and the PP supportive.[ 29 ] It is often argued that the ITT analysis tends to dilute the treatment difference of interest.[ 30 ] Whereas the importance of the ITT population analysis in superiority designs has been well accepted, however there is no consensus about its role in non-inferiority trials.

span.label: and the proposed resolution is to require both and hope they agree - `noninferiority should be concluded ONLY IF BOTH ITT AND PP ANALYSES PERMIT THAT` - which is a procedure rather than a principle, and the paper notes the conservative effect of PP on such trials `has not been thoroughly explored`
span.quote: Therefore, it has been suggested that noninferiority should be concluded only if both ITT and PP analyses permit that.[ 28 31 – 36 ] CPMP guideline states that in a noninferiority trial, the full analysis set based on the ITT principle and the PP analysis set have equal importance and their use should lead to similar conclusions for a robust interpretation.

span.label: **the remedy offered for the missing data ITT cannot ignore is itself contested** - last observation carried forward, `whereby the LAST AVAILABLE MEASUREMENT for each individual at the time point prior to withdrawal IS RETAINED in the analysis`, presented here without its known bias
span.quote: However, in most cases, missing data could also be dealt by using the last observation carried forward (LOCF) method, whereby the last available measurement for each individual at the time point prior to withdrawal from the study is retained in the analysis.

span.quote: Care must always be taken to minimize missing responses and to continue to follow up those who withdraw from treatment. Anyone who follows these principles intelligently and has a vision to minimize bias should not worry further about “intention to treat”.

span.label: the analysis set is defined by the randomized assignment rather than by the treatment actually received, which is what preserves the randomization

span.label: randomisation itself - allocating subjects to arms after eligibility is assessed but before the intervention is given
span.note: eliminates: systematic difference between the groups at baseline; ITT exists to protect this and per-protocol analysis is what spends it · outcome: held
span.quote: ITT analysis reflects the practical clinical scenario because it admits noncompliance and protocol deviations. ITT analysis maintains prognostic balance generated from the original random treatment allocation. It gives an unbiased estimate of treatment effect.

span.label: requiring full reporting of every deviation from random allocation and every missing response, as CONSORT does

span.label: requiring the ITT and per-protocol analyses to agree before a non-inferiority claim is made

span.label: intention-to-treat
span.quote: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) often suffer from two major complications, i.e., noncompliance and missing outcomes. One potential solution to this problem is a statistical concept called intention-to-treat (ITT) concept.

span.label: ITT analysis
span.quote: According to Fisher et al . (1990), the ITT analysis includes all randomized patients in the groups to which they were randomly assigned, regardless of their adherence with the entry criteria, regardless of the treatment they actually received, and regardless of subsequent withdrawal from treatment or deviation from the protocol.

span.label: per-protocol
span.quote: Committee for Proprietary Medicinal Products (CPMP) note for guidance “Biostatistical Methodology in Clinical Trials for Marketing Authorisations for Medicinal Products” states that decisions concerning the analysis population should be guided by the principles underlying the “intention-to-treat” and the “per-protocol” strategies. When the ITT and per-protocol (PP) analyses come to essentially the same conclusions, confidence in the study results is increased.

span.label: modified ITT
span.quote: It is a subset of the ITT population and allows the exclusion of some randomized subjects in a justified way (such as patients who were deemed ineligible after randomization or certain patients who never started treatment). However, the definition given to the modified ITT (mITT) in randomized controlled trial has been found to be irregular and arbitrary because there is a lack of consistent guidelines for its application. The mITT analysis allows a subjective approach in entry criteria, which may lead to confusion, inaccurate results and bias.

span.label: full analysis set
span.quote: The International Conference on Harmonisation (ICH) E9 guideline on “Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials” uses the term “full analysis set” to describe the analysis set which is as complete as possible and as close as possible to the ITT ideal of including all randomized subjects.

span.label: noncompliance
span.quote: ITT analysis avoids overoptimistic estimates of the efficacy of an intervention resulting from the removal of non-compliers by accepting that noncompliance and protocol deviations are likely to occur in actual clinical practice.

span.label: prognostic balance
span.quote: ITT analysis reflects the practical clinical scenario because it admits noncompliance and protocol deviations. ITT analysis maintains prognostic balance generated from the original random treatment allocation. It gives an unbiased estimate of treatment effect.

span.label: type II error
span.quote: ITT analysis has been criticized for being too cautious and thus being more susceptible to type II error.

span.label: sample size
span.quote: ITT analysis preserves the sample size because if noncompliant subjects and dropouts are excluded from the final analysis, it might significantly reduce the sample size, leading to reduced statistical power.

span.label: last observation carried forward
span.quote: However, in most cases, missing data could also be dealt by using the last observation carried forward (LOCF) method, whereby the last available measurement for each individual at the time point prior to withdrawal from the study is retained in the analysis.

span.label: noninferiority
span.quote: Therefore, it has been suggested that noninferiority should be concluded only if both ITT and PP analyses permit that.[ 28 31 – 36 ] CPMP guideline states that in a noninferiority trial, the full analysis set based on the ITT principle and the PP analysis set have equal importance and their use should lead to similar conclusions for a robust interpretation.

span.label: superiority trial
span.quote: CPMP guideline states that for a superiority trial, the ITT analysis should be considered primary and the PP supportive.[ 29 ] It is often argued that the ITT analysis tends to dilute the treatment difference of interest.[ 30 ] Whereas the importance of the ITT population analysis in superiority designs has been well accepted, however there is no consensus about its role in non-inferiority trials.

span.label: heterogeneity
span.quote: Also, heterogeneity might be introduced if noncompliants, dropouts and compliant subjects are mixed together in the final analysis. Moreover, end-point data will differ markedly among noncompliant, dropouts and compliant subjects, and interpretation might become difficult if a large proportion of participants cross over to opposite treatment arms.[ 3 4 12 16 17 ]
